newsitem.title: USA: Feds fear Atlanta festival may present bomb target.
newsitem.headline: Feds fear Atlanta festival may present bomb target.

text.p: Federal agents fear a popular spring festival for black college students in Atlanta could become a target for extremists suspected of carrying out three bombings since July 1996, law enforcement sources say.

Tens of thousands of young blacks from across the country were expected to arrive in Atlanta on April 18 for the annual weekend street party called "Freaknik," an event known for its massive downtown traffic jams and unruly crowds.

This year's festival, officially entitled Black College Spring Break, has raised anxiety levels among federal and state investigators who believe the next bomb attack in Atlanta could be aimed at the minority community.

Further heightening concern is the fact that Freaknik falls on April 19, the fourth anniversary of the catastrophic federal assault on the Branch Davidian compound near Waco, Texas, and the second anniversary of the Oklahoma City bombing.

The date put investigators especially on edge after a militant group called the Army of God claimed responsibility for the bombings of an Atlanta abortion clinic in January and a gay nightclub last month. A letter purported to be from the group threatened new violence and made a specific reference to the burning of the Branch Davidians' Waco compound.
"Freaknik is the biggest potential target. That is, if nothing happens between now and then," one law enforcement officer told Reuters.

Woody Johnson, the special agent in charge of the Atlanta office, said on Thursday that federal, state, county and city police officers have begun behind-the-scenes discussions about the potential risks posed by Freaknik, which in years past has attracted more than 100,000 people with an entertainment itinerary of concerts, sports tournaments and street parties.
"We are exploring the many avenues of pro-active work that we can do to address the potential," he said.
However, the possibility of violence has not worried city officials enough to warn black colleges and universities about the potential danger.

"We are certainly concerned about it," said DeWayne Martin, deputy chief of staff to Atlanta Mayor Bill Campbell. "Our police department is taking all of the precautions necessary to protect citizens and visitors during the weekend."
Authorities were expected reimplement an inter-agency command structure set up to provide security during the Olympic Games last summer.

The Games became Atlanta's first bombing target on the morning of July 27, 1996, when a pipe-bomb exploded at a crowded outdoor concert in Centennial Olympic Park, leaving two people dead and more than 100 injured. A phone warning from an anonymous caller reached officers late because of a flaw in the city's 911 emergency telephone service.
The abortion clinic and gay nightclub bombings injured about a dozen people.

Federal investigators still cannot say definitively whether the bombings were connected. But law enforcement sources and hate crime experts believe those responsible to be extremists, possibly tied to the citizens' militia movement or white supremacist groups such as Christian Identity and the Phineas Priesthood.
The black makeup of Freaknik could serve as effective protection against would-be white supremacist bombers, however.

"This particular bomber appears to be white and may worry about how he stands out in a progressive type of environment," said Brian Levin, who heads the Centre on Hate and Extremism at Richard Stockton College in Ponoma, New Jersey.
